Polygon's Latest Tambora Gravel Bike Stands As Their Lightest and Fastest – Priced As Low as $1,800
11 photos
Photo: Polygon Bikes
Bicycles have always been one of the go-to solutions for moving around our cities and over the years, they’ve changed drastically. Even now, trends are taking the cycling world by storm, and we’re about to witness how.
For years, the trusted hardtail MTB was the average Joe’s go-to bicycle, being seem ridden around town, on dirt roads, and even through mountain trails. I remember riding my own to school, to grab groceries, and on the weekends, even hit up some desert trails in Phoenix. However, the past few years have seen the introduction of a different kind of all-rounder bicycle: the gravel bike.
Instead of building the do-it-all spirit around a frame that is technically born to handle woodlands, the gravel frame started off with what is essentially a road-bike, one with a traditional diamond frame, stiff front fork, and even drop bars. Often, gravel tires are narrower than what we see on an MTB, but recent trends are changing all that.
Photo: Polygon Bikes Considering most of us do their riding on tarmac, it just made sense to build a bike upon a design and style that is at home in that very setting. Some differences between a road and gravel bike are also very clear, with one in particular acting as a way to soften up the rear: dropping the seat stays. This allows the seat post to move a bit more freely while also minimizing the size of the rear triangle; the latter also adds more compliance.
Another trait gravel bikes are known for is the presence of drop bars, and since these bikes are often ridden in settings that offer more vibrations and instability than tarmac, handlebar flare is integrated to widen our grip and provide stability. Flares can also cause the body to sit a tad more upright than on a road bike, not to mention the use of risers and different stems.
As the years have gone by, and the gravel bike exposed to more and more R&D, it too has begun to change, with some brands even going as far as integrating fork travel into the design, and even flat bars or straight handlebars, as we often see on MTBs . Teams like SRAM even have dedicated suspension forks for gravel, not to mention entire drivetrain ranges.
Photo: Polygon Bikes All that brings us to the ravishing beast before us today: Polygon Bikes’ latest spin on the gravel ecosystem. What this crew has done here is set their sights on a much more modern and sportier gravel bike, one that even taps into aero tricks and traits we often see on road bikes in order to help riders shave seconds off the clocks. Sources mention that this ones is to now stand as Tambora’s gravel racing flagship.
Furthermore, four separate builds also position the frame to land in the hands of as many people as possible, with prices ranging from under $2,000, $1,800, to be precise, to $4,500, so a bit of everything for everyone, and yes, all use the latest and “lightest gravel platform” this team has ever brought to the market.
While weights for the complete bikes are not mentioned on the manufacturer’s website, sources state that the new frame does weighs just 1,200 grams and can handle a total load of 125 kg (276 lbs).
Photo: Polygon Bikes It’s called ACX, and this carbon fiber frame has been specifically designed to push as much power into that rear wheel as possible while also keeping rider fatigue to a minimum. The geo has been updated to place us in a much more aggressive and aerodynamic position and the wheelbase lengthened for stability.
In terms of compatibility, the new platform can be equipped with 1x or 2x drivetrains, and handles wheels as large as 55 c or nearly 2.2 inches of rubber. That’s the size of tires on some MTBs.
Yet, the real treat that gravel riders can look forward to is the ability to use a suspension fork on this frame, allowing us to keep up with trends and creating a bicycle that really can be the go-to choice for most riding settings. Forks with up to 40 mm of travel are on the menu for this one and dropper posts too.
One little component that I want to attract your attention to is the down tube. Okay, so the Tambora’s down tube is not little, and that’s precisely what I want to point out; there’s a reason for its size.
Photo: Polygon Bikes Aside from the shape of the tube, which just screams “I can take what you throw at me,” and also a bit aerodynamic, it’s also where Polygon now integrates the PolyPocket storage system. We can bring along a kit for flats, tools, gels, and other “stuff.”
Yet, Polygon did not sacrifice mounts on the new platform, and for those of use that use gravel bikes to ride to the edge of town and beyond, camping out under the stars in the process, be happy to know that we find mounts all over the frameset. The fork has them, the seat tube has them and the down tube too, but lacks mounts for fenders; this one’s dirty!
Personally, I’d love taking this beast out for a spin, and with complete bikes starting at $1,800, most of us are sure to be thinking the same thing. In time, you can add better components to it and still end up with a $4,500 ride after a year of pumping cash into it. Nice!
